interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through what happens in a typical 45-minute coding interview, start to finish.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It runs in roughly five phases, and I pace against them rather than letting the clock surprise me. First two or three minutes are intro and the problem gets read out or shared. Then I spend three to five minutes on **clarifying questions** — input size, duplicates, ordering, what counts as invalid input — before committing to an approach.

Next is five to ten minutes talking through an approach, usually starting from a brute force and narrating why I'd improve it, landing on something I state a complexity for before I start typing. Coding itself gets fifteen to twenty minutes, and I try to keep talking while I type rather than going silent.

The last chunk, five to ten minutes, is testing: I pick two or three cases that stress the logic — empty input, a duplicate, the largest size — and trace them by hand rather than declaring "looks good." Whatever's left goes to questions I have for the interviewer.

The biggest risk in this shape is spending too long in the approach phase and running out of runway to test, so I actively watch the clock at the fifteen-minute mark and force a decision if I'm still debating approaches.

**Testing:** whether you understand the round has a real internal structure you can manage, versus treating the whole 45 minutes as one undifferentiated block.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: You wrote a fully correct, efficient solution but got rejected anyway. What do you think went wrong, and how would you approach the next round differently?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My honest read: correctness is only one of four things being scored, and a correct-but-silent solution leaves no evidence for the other three — communication, complexity reasoning, and code quality. The written debrief the interviewer files afterward can't credit thinking it never observed, and a silent-but-correct answer is indistinguishable on paper from a memorized one.

Concretely, if I solved a two-pointer problem without saying a word, the interviewer has no record of whether I recognized the pattern or got lucky pattern-matching from practice. Next round, I'd deliberately produce that evidence: state the brute force out loud even if I skip straight to the better approach, name the complexity before I'm asked, and narrate the two or three edge cases I'm testing against instead of just running them silently.

I'd also flag trade-offs unprompted — "this is O(n) time but O(n) extra space; I could trade that for O(1) space with a different pointer scheme if that mattered here." That single sentence covers complexity and judgment in one breath.

The code doesn't need to change. What needs to change is making the thinking behind it visible in real time.

**Testing:** whether you can self-diagnose a confusing rejection instead of concluding the bar is arbitrary or that you simply need harder practice problems.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging your own performance

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prepare differently for a phone screen versus a full onsite loop at the same company?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat the phone screen as a filter, not a preview of the loop, so I prep for speed and clean fundamentals rather than depth. It's usually one problem in 30 to 45 minutes with one interviewer who's screening for "can this person code at all," so I make sure my basics — array/string manipulation, hash maps, simple recursion — are fast and clean, and I don't over-invest time explaining things that aren't in question.

For the onsite loop, I prep assuming each round is scored independently by a different interviewer with their own rubric interpretation, and that follow-ups will push into a second or third variant of the same problem. I spend more time practicing the follow-up muscle — "now it's a stream," "now there are duplicates" — because escalation inside one round is more common at onsite than a phone screen, where there's rarely time for it.

One mistake I avoid: bringing onsite-level exhaustiveness to a phone screen. Spending ten minutes clarifying every edge case on a 30-minute screen can burn the exact time the screen is testing you use well. I match depth to the stage's actual purpose.

**Testing:** whether you understand the stages serve different evaluation goals, rather than prepping for "a coding interview" as one undifferentiated event.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Preparation strategy

interviewQuestions.question: As a senior or staff candidate, how does the format and what's expected of you change compared to earlier in your career?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The problem itself usually gets harder faster, or the interviewer folds in architectural follow-ups — "how would this scale across machines" — because raw problem-solving ability is assumed rather than tested at that level. What I actually think is being probed is whether I question the problem's framing instead of accepting it at face value, and whether my code still looks like something I'd ship even under time pressure.

Concretely, if given an ambiguous prompt, I'll push back on an assumption baked into it — "you said 'find duplicates' but didn't say if the input is sorted; that changes whether I need O(n) extra space at all" — rather than silently picking an interpretation. That kind of framing challenge is rare from junior candidates and is part of what separates the rounds.

I also keep the boring parts of the code intact: real variable names, a guard clause for the empty-input case, a small helper function instead of one dense block — because a staff engineer's code in production isn't shortcuts, and an interviewer watching for that signal notices immediately when it's missing.

The risk at this level is over-indexing on being fast and under-indexing on demonstrating judgment, which is the actual thing being hired for.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate what changes about the bar at your own level, which is itself a form of seniority signal.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Staff-level signal
